title: Bitter Root
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 2 of 40
content:
By the second morning, Severus Snape had decided that I was incompetent in seven distinct ways.

He informed me of each one before breakfast.

The first involved my labeling system.

The second involved my knife.

The third involved what he called “an inexplicable emotional attachment to Ministry-approved storage protocols.”

By the time he reached the seventh, I had stopped defending myself and begun taking notes.

He noticed.

“What are you writing?”

“Your complaints.”

“Why?”

“I like complete records.”

His eyes narrowed.

I turned the clipboard around.

Under TODAY'S ERRORS, I had written:

1. Existing alphabetically.
2. Owning a knife with a Ministry inspection stamp.
3. Believing labels should face outward.
4. Breathing too loudly near dried hellebore.
5. Possessing optimism regarding inventory forms.
6. Moving a stool three inches to the left.
7. Unknown. Subject became distracted by tea.

Snape read the list.

His expression did not change.

His left eyebrow rose by perhaps half an inch.

“You omitted your most serious failing.”

“Which is?”

“Encouraging yourself.”

I added it as number eight.

A sound escaped him.

Not a laugh exactly. More a sharp exhale that had taken a wrong turn.

I pretended not to notice.

That, I was learning, was often the kindest thing I could do for him.

The hidden phials from the previous day now sat inside a containment box on the central table. I had slept badly because of them. Snape, judging by the shadows under his eyes, had not slept at all.

McGonagall wanted them turned over to the Ministry.

Snape wanted them analyzed first.

I agreed with Snape, which he seemed to consider suspicious.

“You are not required to indulge me,” he said.

“I am not indulging you.”

“You are delaying an evidence transfer.”

“I am documenting the evidence properly.”

“The distinction is bureaucratic.”

“The distinction is whether the Ministry knows what it is holding before someone drops a phial in an evidence room.”

His gaze flicked toward me.

“You disapprove of the Ministry.”

“I disapprove of institutions that believe forms prevent stupidity.”

“An unexpectedly reasonable position.”

“Careful. That was nearly a compliment.”

“Then let us agree never to speak of it again.”

We worked in silence.

The potion inside the first phial was dark red, almost black. Under magnification, silver threads moved through it like veins of moonlight. Snape watched while I drew a sample into a charmed pipette.

“Do not heat it,” he said.

“I wasn't planning to.”

“You were looking at the burner.”

“I was looking past the burner.”

“At what?”

“The cabinet.”

“Why?”

“I enjoy cabinets.”

He gave me a flat look.

“Fine,” I said. “I was considering heating it.”

“I know.”

“How?”

“Your thumb moved.”

I glanced at my hand.

“My thumb.”

“You reach for the striker with your right hand. You flex your thumb immediately before doing so.”

I stared at him.

He stared back.

“Do you observe everyone like this?” I asked.

“Yes.”

“That sounds exhausting.”

“It is usually disappointing.”

There was no way to tell whether he was joking.

I was beginning to enjoy that.

We tested the sample cold. Sopophorous residue. Powdered asphodel. A binding agent I did not recognize. Something bitter enough to sting through the detection charm.

Snape leaned closer.

His shoulder brushed mine.

Both of us stopped.

The contact had been accidental and barely there, yet his body locked as though I had drawn a wand.

I moved half a step away.

He said nothing.

Neither did I.

After a moment, he pointed at the silver threads. “That is not part of the original formulation.”

“Original?”

His mouth flattened.

“Voldemort wanted a compliance draught that left the subject capable of speech and movement while reducing resistance. Crude people prefer crude solutions. The Imperius Curse left evidence in trained minds. He wanted something quieter.”

The words chilled me more than the dungeon.

“And you made it?”

“I was instructed to.”

“That isn't what I asked.”

His eyes cut toward mine.

“No,” he said at last. “I made something that looked as though it would work.”

I studied the sample again.

“The binding agent.”

“Bitterroot resin.”

“That would destabilize the asphodel.”

“Yes.”

“Slowly.”

“Yes.”

“So the potion would pass a surface test.”

“And fail after several hours.”

I looked at him.

He had arranged his face into indifference, but his right hand was gripping his sleeve.

“How many?” I asked.

“How many what?”

“How many things like this did you sabotage?”

“I did not keep a tally for future admirers.”

“I am not admiring you.”

“Your restraint is heroic.”

“I'm trying to understand the stock.”

“No. You are trying to understand me.”

The accusation landed cleanly.

I set down the pipette.

“Fine,” I said. “A little.”

His expression sharpened.

“You are a man who was publicly believed to be Voldemort's loyal servant. Now I keep finding evidence that you spent years quietly breaking the machinery around him. That is professionally relevant.”

“And personally fascinating?”

“Annoying, actually.”

His brow furrowed.

“You don't fit neatly in the categories.”

“I shall endeavor to be simpler for your convenience.”

“Don't. Simple people are terrible company.”

For the first time, I caught him completely unprepared.

His face went blank in a way that was not Occlumency. It was surprise.

Then he looked away.

“Bitterroot,” he said. “There should be some in the lower cabinet.”

I let him change the subject.

The root was exactly where he said it would be, wrapped in waxed paper and tied with black thread. When I sliced it, the cut surface immediately darkened.

Snape watched my knife technique.

“You are holding it incorrectly.”

“I've been doing this for years.”

“So have people who play bagpipes.”

“What does that have to do with anything?”

“Longevity does not prove merit.”

I handed him the knife.

“Show me.”

His eyes narrowed, as if he suspected a trap.

Then he took it.

Even injured, his hands changed when he worked.

The tremor disappeared beneath concentration. His fingers were long and pale, the nails stained faintly from years of ingredients no soap could entirely remove. He adjusted his grip, placed the blade against the root, and cut at an angle so shallow I almost missed the motion.

“More surface area,” he said.

“And less crushed fiber.”

“Obviously.”

I smiled.

His eyes lifted.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You are smirking.”

“I would never.”

“You are doing it now.”

“Perhaps your observational skills are deteriorating.”

He handed the knife back with unnecessary precision.

“Again.”

I copied the cut.

“Too deep.”

Again.

“Your wrist.”

Again.

“Better.”

I glanced at him.

His lips pressed together.

“That was a compliment,” I said.

“It was an assessment.”

“I'm writing it down.”

“If you do, I will burn the clipboard.”

“You'd have to catch me.”

His eyes went to the cane leaning against his chair.

Mine followed.

The joke collapsed between us.

I wished immediately that I could take it back.

Snape's face closed.

I set the knife down.

“That was careless,” I said. “I'm sorry.”

He looked at me for a long moment.

Most people, I suspected, filled that kind of silence around him. They explained themselves. They softened the apology. They insisted they had not meant it.

I waited.

At last he said, “Yes. It was.”

Then he took the bitterroot from me and resumed slicing.

It was not forgiveness.

It was, somehow, better.

We worked until noon.

The first phial proved useless as a compliance draught. The second did too. By the fourth, a pattern emerged: every batch contained a different flaw, subtle enough to survive a hurried inspection and severe enough to ruin the intended effect.

Snape had not simply refused Voldemort.

He had made obedience look like competence.

At lunch, McGonagall sent sandwiches and a note asking whether the phials could be transferred.

I wrote back: NOT YET. ACTIVE ANALYSIS IN PROGRESS.

Snape read over my shoulder.

“You enjoy provoking authority.”

“I enjoy accurate punctuation.”

“That sentence contained neither rebellion nor punctuation.”

“I know. It will keep her guessing.”

This time the sound he made was unquestionably a laugh.

It was brief, rough from the injury to his throat, and gone almost before I could be sure I had heard it.

Snape froze.

I picked up my sandwich.

“Number nine,” I said, looking at my clipboard.

His eyes narrowed.

“Eating in the laboratory.”

His mouth twitched.

“Finally,” he said, “you have identified a genuine failing.”

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
